newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS-Finland presents balanced budget, EMU on course.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Finland presents balanced budget, EMU on course.

text.p: Finland's 1997 state budget presented on Tuesday is the country's first balanced budget since 1990 and paves the way for participation in monetary union, the government said.

The economic scenario outlined by the finance ministry and the balance achieved in the core budget paved the way for Finland's entry to the EMU currency union in the first wave in 1997, the government said in its budget document.
"Finland has good prospects for fulfilling the convergence criteria in 1997," it added.
"Next year, we need to borrow only to pay interest on old debts," finance ministry budget chief Erkki Virtanen told a news conference.
For the first time since 1990, the core of the budget is in balance, with state revenue excluding borrowing at the same level as state expenditure excluding debt servicing.

"It is a budget of confidence," Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen commented on national television on Tuesday morning, a sentiment echoed by Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto who said his first budget was "one of confidence and hope".
Features of the 1997 budget include income tax reductions worth 5.5 billion markka ($1.22 billion) which the Social Democratic-led coalition government hopes will boost private consumption.
The tax reductions -- timed to take effect ahead of local elections in October -- will also divert attention from a continued drive to reduce expenditure.
Spending cuts will trim the budget by about 16 billion markka next year, the government said in its budget document.

Total state spending -- which includes non-budget items such as construction subsidies, pension funds and state bank guarantees -- will fall to 200.4 billion markka in 1997 from 212.9 billion in 1996.
Budget spending will be 190.8 billion markka, but Virtanen said 1997 outlays cannot be compared with earlier years due to technical accounting changes.
"It looks like the (1997) net financing requirement for state finances will remain below 30 billion markka," he said, adding that figure included items outside the actual budget.
State debt servicing costs, now the second-largest spending item after social and health affairs, will rise to 31 billion markka next year from 29.3 billion in 1996, Virtanen said.

Even so, a decreasing need for new borrowing would gradually bring the steep rise in state indebtedness to a halt, the government said, forecasting its state debt to GDP ratio at 71.9 percent in 1997, up from just 10 percent in 1990.
The ratio would begin to decline after 1997, the government said, and a new 1996-97 economic forecast from the finance ministry radiated increased confidence.
"Economic growth is expected to be vigorous in 1997," the ministry said in a statement.

GDP growth would accelerate to 3.9 percent in 1997 from 2.6 percent this year. Domestic demand would be strong but inflation would remain low and the current account would show a healthy surplus, the ministry said.
"We have stabilised the economy," Prime Minister Lipponen told national television, adding that the private and public sectors should now feel confident about investing.
The government pointed to a fall of almost three percentage points in long bond yields since it took office in spring 1995.

"In the future, economic growth can be rapid without a risk of unbalanced price, monetary or foreign trade developments," it said, adding Finnish net foreign debt to GDP would fall further to about 20 percent by the end of the decade.
The only cloud on the horizon was unemployment. The jobless rate would fall by only one percentage point by 1997 from its current level of 16.4 percent.
($1=4.50 Markka)
